Medcouple

Source: R/medcouple.R
medcouple.Rd

This function calculates the medcouple (MC), a robust measure of the skewness of a distribution (Brys et al. 2004), for a numeric vector or for each column of a matrix or data frame, such as one medcouple per wavelength of a set of spectra.

Usage

medcouple(x, drop_na = FALSE)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector, or a numeric matrix, data frame or tibble (one medcouple per column).

drop_na

Logical value indicating whether to remove missing values (NA). If FALSE (default), the medcouple of a vector or column that contains missing values is NA.

Value

For a vector, the medcouple of x. For a matrix or data frame, a numeric vector with the medcouple of each column, named by the columns. The medcouple of a vector without values is NA.

Details

The medcouple is the median of the kernel $$h(x_i, x_j) = \frac{(x_j - m) - (m - x_i)}{x_j - x_i}$$ over all the pairs of observations \(x_i \le m \le x_j\) with \(x_i \ne x_j\), where \(m\) is the median of the data (with a special definition of \(h\) for the ties at the median). It compares the distances to the median of the observations above and below it, scaled by their distance from each other, so it is unchanged by a shift or a rescaling of the data.

The interpretation of the medcouple is as follows:

  • It lies between -1 and 1, and is 0 for a symmetric distribution.

  • Positive values indicate a right-skewed distribution (a longer upper tail), and negative values a left-skewed one.

Unlike the classical skewness, which is based on the third moment and can be driven by a single extreme value, the medcouple has a breakdown value of 25%. It is computed by robustbase::mc(), in \(O(n \log n)\) time. The medcouple is used by the adjusted boxplot (adjusted_boxplot()) and the skewness-adjusted fences of iqr_outliers(); medcouple_weight() applies it to each half of the data to measure the weight of the tails.

For spectra, one medcouple per wavelength describes the shape of the distribution of the intensities at each channel. Channels that saturate the detector in many spectra have a strongly negative medcouple, since their intensities pile up at the top of the range, while the lines of an element whose contents are skewed, with a few samples far above the others, have a positive one.

References

  • Brys, G., Hubert, M., and Struyf, A. (2004). A robust measure of skewness. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 13(4):996-1017

  • Hubert, M., and Vandervieren, E. (2008). An adjusted boxplot for skewed distributions. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 52(12):5186-5201

See also

medcouple_weight(), adjusted_boxplot(), iqr_outliers(), summary_stats()

Author

Christian L. Goueguel

Examples

data(forageLIBS)
# iron contents (mg/kg): a few samples are far above the others
fe <- forageLIBS$Fe[!is.na(forageLIBS$Fe)]
moments::skewness(fe)   # classical, driven by the highest contents
#> [1] 3.921052
medcouple(fe)           # robust
#> [1] 0.4230769

# one medcouple per column; Fe and Zn have a few missing values
contents <- forageLIBS[c("Ca", "K", "Mg", "P", "Fe", "Mn", "Zn")]
round(medcouple(contents, drop_na = TRUE), 2)
#>   Ca    K   Mg    P   Fe   Mn   Zn 
#> 0.14 0.06 0.02 0.01 0.42 0.19 0.22 

# one medcouple per wavelength, from 380 to 430 nm
wl <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(names(forageLIBS)))
mc <- medcouple(forageLIBS[which(wl > 380 & wl < 430)])
summary(mc)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#> -0.84580 -0.02255  0.02165  0.01979  0.07228  0.32800 
# the Ca II line at 393.37 nm saturates the detector (65535 counts) in
# most spectra: a negative medcouple; the Fe I line at 404.58 nm follows
# the skewed iron contents: a positive one
wl <- as.numeric(names(mc))
round(mc[c(which.min(abs(wl - 393.37)), which.min(abs(wl - 404.58)))], 2)
#> 393.3599236 404.6139835 
#>       -0.83        0.20
